title: Modifiers; adjectives vs adverbs
blurb: Fix misplaced and dangling modifiers, choose adjective or adverb (good or well, bad or badly), and use comparisons, fewer and less correctly.
question: An applicant's essay says, “Rushing to the clinic, the bus left without me. I felt real tired, but I still did good on my shift.” What is wrong with each sentence, and how should it read?

teach.h: Modifiers must sit next to what they describe
teach.body: Formally, a modifier is a word, phrase or clause that describes another word. Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. A modifier must be placed next to the word it modifies, and that word must actually appear in the sentence. Plain English: a describing word sticks to its nearest neighbor, so put it beside the right one, or the sentence says something you never meant.

rows.label: Problem
values: Target word is too far away

rows.label: Example
values: Served soup to patients in bowls
Walking in, the lights were bright

teach.caption: Fixed: “She served soup in bowls to the patients.” “Walking into the clinic, Ana noticed the bright lights.”

steps.label: Spot the opener
steps.sub: Walking in, / To pass the test, / After eating,

teach.caption: The subject right after an introductory phrase must be the one doing the action in that phrase.

teach.note: Only, just, almost, nearly and even go directly before the word they limit.

head: Type
Modifies
Example
rows: a careful nurse; she is quick
a really good result (not real good)
I feel bad. It tastes sour.
teach.caption: Linking verbs (be, feel, seem, look, taste, smell, sound) connect the subject to an adjective: “It tastes sour,” “I feel bad.” Merriam-Webster also accepts “I feel badly,” so that one is a preference, not an error.

teach.body: Good is an adjective: “a good result,” “The soup tastes good.” Well is an adverb: “She did well on the exam,” “The wound is healing well.” Well is also an adjective meaning healthy: “I feel well today.” So after an action verb (did, slept, healed, performed) the answer is always well, never good.

teach.h: Comparing two vs three or more
head: Base
Two things
Three or more
teach.caption: Never double up: not “more better,” not “most fastest.” “The better of the two,” “the best of the three.”

teach.note: Fix double negatives with one negative: can hardly, don't have any.

teach.body: Nursing applicant Tyler Nguyen wrote: “Rushing to the clinic, the bus left without me. I felt real tired, but I still did good on my shift.” The opener “Rushing to the clinic” dangles: the bus was not rushing. Fix: “Rushing to the clinic, I watched the bus leave without me.” Real is modifying the adjective tired, so it must be the adverb really. Did is an action verb, so it takes the adverb well. Final: “I felt really tired, but I still did well on my shift.”

teach.text: Dangling modifiers sound fine when you read fast, because your brain fills in the doer. On the TEAS, always check the first noun after an introductory phrase: if it cannot do the action (lights cannot walk, care cannot pass a test), the modifier dangles.

items: Place modifiers next to what they modify; put only, just, almost, nearly right before the word they limit.
After an introductory phrase, the subject must be the doer of that phrase's action.
Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and adverbs (really good, not real good).
Linking verbs take adjectives (feel bad); action verbs take adverbs (did well).
Two things: -er/more; three or more: -est/most; never double comparisons.
Fewer and number for countables; less and amount for uncountables; no double negatives.

summary: You can now spot and fix misplaced and dangling modifiers and place limiting words precisely. You can also choose adjectives or adverbs correctly, form comparisons for two versus three or more, and use fewer and less without error.

A.q: Which sentence is free of a dangling modifier?
options: Hurrying to the lab, Devon dropped the sample tray.
Hurrying to the lab, the sample tray fell to the floor.
Hurrying to the lab, the tray slipped from Devon's hands.
Hurrying to the lab, the samples were dropped by Devon.
A.why: Devon is the one hurrying, and he is the subject right after the introductory phrase.

whyNot.1: The tray becomes the subject, so the sentence says the tray was hurrying.
whyNot.2: The tray is still the subject; Devon appears only as a possessive, not as the doer.
whyNot.3: The passive voice makes the samples the subject; Devon is not the doer after the comma.

A.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “The patient said she feels ___ today, and her incision is healing ___.”
options: well / good
good / good
well / well
nicely / well
A.why: Well as an adjective means healthy after the linking verb feels, and well as an adverb modifies the action verb healing.

whyNot.0: Healing is an action verb and needs the adverb well, not the adjective good.
whyNot.1: Healing good is wrong: action verbs take adverbs.
whyNot.3: Feels is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective; nicely is an adverb.

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The night shift has ___ nurses than the day shift.”
options: less
fewer
lesser
more fewer
A.why: Nurses can be counted, so fewer is correct.

whyNot.0: Less is for uncountable amounts (less water), not countable nurses.
whyNot.2: Lesser means lower in importance or quality, not a smaller number.
whyNot.3: More fewer is a double comparison.

B.q: Ray wants to say that he slept four hours and no more before the exam. Which sentence says this most clearly?
options: Only Ray slept four hours before the exam.
Ray slept four hours before the only exam.
Ray slept four hours before the exam only.
Ray slept only four hours before the exam.
B.why: Only sits directly before four hours, the amount it limits.

whyNot.0: Only before Ray means nobody else slept four hours.
whyNot.1: Only before exam suggests there was just one exam, which is a different meaning.
whyNot.2: Only at the end limits the time: he slept four hours before the exam and at no other time.

B.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Of the three practice tests, the second one was the ___.”
options: harder
most hard
hardest
more harder
B.why: Three items call for the superlative. Hard is one syllable, so it takes -est: hardest.

whyNot.0: Harder is the comparative, used for two items, not three.
whyNot.1: One-syllable adjectives add -est rather than using most.
whyNot.3: More harder is a double comparison, and it is also the comparative form.

B.q: The sticker has a smiley face on it. Which sentence places the modifier correctly?
options: The nurse gave the boy a sticker with a smiley face.
The nurse gave a sticker to the boy with a smiley face.
With a smiley face, the nurse gave the boy a sticker.
The nurse with a smiley face gave the boy a sticker.
B.why: “With a smiley face” sits right after sticker, the word it describes.

whyNot.1: The phrase now sits next to boy, so the boy seems to have the smiley face.
whyNot.2: The opening phrase attaches to the nurse, the subject after the comma.
whyNot.3: The phrase directly describes the nurse.

C.q: Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
options: The new graduate did real good on her first review.
The cough syrup tastes badly, but it works quickly.
She charted careful so the next shift could follow.
The rash looks worse today than it did yesterday.
C.why: Looks is a linking verb, so it takes an adjective; worse is the correct comparative of bad for two days.

whyNot.0: Real should be the adverb really, and did good should be did well.
whyNot.1: Tastes is a linking verb and takes an adjective: tastes bad.
whyNot.2: Charted is an action verb and needs the adverb carefully.

C.q: Which revision corrects the dangling modifier in “To pass the TEAS, careful study is required”?
options: To pass the TEAS, careful study is required by students.
To pass the TEAS, students need careful study.
To pass the TEAS, it requires careful study.
To pass the TEAS, a careful study plan is needed.
C.why: Students are the ones who will pass the TEAS, and they are now the subject right after the opening phrase.

whyNot.0: Careful study is still the subject, so study seems to be passing the TEAS.
whyNot.2: It has no clear antecedent and cannot pass a test.
whyNot.3: A study plan is now the subject, and a plan cannot pass the TEAS.

C.q: Which sentence avoids a double negative?
options: The patient can't hardly sleep because of the noise.
The patient doesn't have no appetite this morning.
The patient can barely sleep because of the noise.
The patient couldn't scarcely eat anything at dinner.
C.why: Barely is the only negative word, so the sentence is correct.

whyNot.0: Can't and hardly are both negatives; use can hardly.
whyNot.1: Doesn't and no are both negatives; use doesn't have any.
whyNot.3: Couldn't and scarcely are both negatives; use could scarcely.

reteach.title: Modifiers are magnets
reteach.question: Picture every describing word as a small magnet. It sticks to whatever is closest. What goes wrong when the wrong thing is closest, or when nothing is there at all?

blocks.h: It sticks to the nearest neighbor
blocks.body: Put the magnet “with a smiley face” next to boy and the boy gets the smiley face. Put it next to sticker and the sticker does. A dangling modifier is a magnet with nothing to stick to: “After eating lunch, the shift started” has no person who ate, so the magnet grabs the shift. Always place the magnet against the right word, and make sure that word is in the sentence.

rows.label: Misplaced
values: the boy with a smiley face
a sticker with a smiley face

rows.label: Dangling
values: After lunch, Jo began her shift

rows.label: Limiting
values: I almost read all of it
I read almost all of it

blocks.text: Moving the opener to passive voice (“bright lights were noticed by Ana”) does not fix a dangling modifier: the doer must be the subject right after the comma.

explain.body: Put each modifier beside the word it describes. Limiting words (only, just, almost, nearly, even) go directly before the word they limit, and moving them changes the meaning.

test.q: Carlos finished most of the charts but not all of them. Which sentence says this clearly?
options: Carlos almost finished all of the charts.
Carlos finished almost all of the charts.
Carlos finished all of the charts almost.
Almost Carlos finished all of the charts.
test.why: Almost sits directly before all, so it limits the number of charts: most, but not every one, were finished.

whyNot.0: Almost before finished limits the action, saying he came close to finishing rather than telling how many he finished.
whyNot.2: Almost at the end is misplaced and leaves the meaning unclear.
whyNot.3: Almost before Carlos limits Carlos, which makes no sense.

explain.body: An introductory phrase with no subject of its own borrows the subject after the comma. If that subject cannot do the action, the modifier dangles. Fix it by naming the doer as the subject.

rows.label: Example
values: After eating, Jo began her shift.

test.q: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
options: After finishing the shift, Rae drove home.
After Rae finished her long shift, she drove home.
After finishing the shift, Rae felt tired.
After finishing the shift, the drive felt long.
test.why: The drive is the subject after the comma, but a drive cannot finish a shift. The doer (Rae) is missing.

whyNot.0: Rae finished the shift and is the subject, so the modifier is attached correctly.
whyNot.1: The opener is a full clause with its own subject (Rae), so nothing dangles.
whyNot.2: Rae finished the shift and is the subject, so the modifier is attached correctly.

explain.body: Action verbs take adverbs (did well, works carefully). Linking verbs such as feel, look, seem and taste take adjectives (feel bad, looks good). Well can also be an adjective meaning healthy.

test.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “I don't feel ___ today, and I didn't sleep ___ last night.”
options: well / well
well / good
good / good
nicely / well
test.why: Feel well (healthy) uses well as an adjective; sleep well uses well as an adverb with the action verb sleep.

whyNot.1: Sleep is an action verb and needs the adverb well, not good.
whyNot.2: Sleep good is wrong: action verbs take adverbs.
whyNot.3: Feel is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective; nicely is an adverb.

explain.body: Use -er/more for two things and -est/most for three or more, never both together. Use fewer and number with things you can count, less and amount with things you cannot.

test.q: Which sentence about two nursing programs is correct?
options: Of the two programs, Riverside is the best choice.
Of the two programs, Riverside is the more better choice.
Of the two programs, Riverside has the less applicants.
Of the two programs, Riverside is the better choice.
test.why: Two programs call for the comparative better.

whyNot.0: Best is the superlative, for three or more.
whyNot.1: More better is a double comparison.
whyNot.2: Applicants are countable, so it should be fewer applicants.
